Core Philosophy: The Argument for Elimination

The fundamental argument for eliminating zoning rests on two pillars:

  1. Property Rights: Zoning is viewed as a government infringement on an individual's right to use their land as they see fit, so long as they do not create a tangible nuisance (e.g., pollution, noise) that harms others. Proponents argue that peaceful, voluntary use of property should not be restricted by government decree.
  2. Market Efficiency: Proponents believe that a free market in land use is far more efficient at allocating resources (in this case, housing and commercial space) than central planning by a government body. They argue zoning creates artificial scarcity, distorts prices, and stifles innovation.

Supposed Benefits and Improvements

1. Drastically Improved Housing Availability & Affordability

This is the most cited benefit. The argument is that zoning is the primary cause of housing shortages in desirable cities.

  • Elimination of Artificial Scarcity: Zoning laws, particularly those that mandate low-density single-family housing (R1 zoning), create an artificial cap on the number of housing units that can be built. By removing this cap, the market would be free to respond to high demand with increased supply. Developers could build taller apartment buildings, subdivide large lots, and add missing middle housing (duplexes, triplexes, townhomes) in any neighborhood where it is economically feasible.
  • Reduced Construction Costs: Zoning often comes with onerous requirements like minimum lot sizes, parking mandates, set-backs, and lengthy approval processes. Eliminating these would reduce the cost and time to build, savings that could be passed on to buyers and renters.
  • Meeting Real Demand: The market would naturally provide the types of housing people actually want and can afford at that location. Instead of being forced to choose only between a single-family home or a large apartment complex, a wider variety of options would emerge to meet different income levels and family sizes.

2. Enhanced Economic Growth and Mobility

  • Labor Market Flexibility: When housing is cheap and abundant in economically vibrant cities, people can move more freely to pursue jobs. This reduces unemployment and allows businesses to access a larger pool of workers, boosting overall economic productivity.
  • Reduced Commutes & Transportation Costs: Without strict separation of uses, people could live closer to where they work, shop, and socialize. This would lead to more walkable, mixed-use neighborhoods, reducing traffic congestion, transportation expenses, and environmental impacts.
  • Entrepreneurship and Innovation: Removing restrictions on home-based businesses and commercial uses would lower the barrier to entry for entrepreneurs. It could allow for more small-scale retail, cafes, and workshops integrated into residential areas, revitalizing neighborhoods.

3. Stronger Protection of Property Rights

  • Self-Determination: Libertarians argue that a landowner should have the maximum freedom to use their property without needing permission from the government or their neighbors, unless their actions constitute a direct violation of others' rights (handled by common law nuisance suits, not preemptive regulation).
  • Reduced Bureaucracy and Corruption: The zoning approval process is often politicized, slow, and susceptible to NIMBYism ("Not In My Backyard") where a vocal minority can block beneficial projects. Eliminating zoning would remove this discretionary power from planning boards and city councils, reducing opportunities for corruption and streamlining development.

4. More Organic and Adaptive Urban Design

  • Evolutionary Development: Cities would develop more organically based on actual human behavior and economic patterns, rather than a static, decades-old plan. Neighborhoods could adapt more quickly to changing demographics and economic conditions.
  • Historical Precedent: Proponents point to pre-zoning cities (like early 20th century New York or Houston before the 1990s) which developed dense, mixed-use, and vibrant neighborhoods naturally. Houston is often used as an example; while it has land use regulations (e.g., parking mandates, lot size rules), it famously lacks traditional zoning and has historically had more affordable housing than many coastal cities with strict zoning.

Important Criticisms and Counterpoints (The Other Side of the Coin)

It is crucial to understand the arguments against complete elimination:

  • Negative Externalities (Nuisances): The most significant fear is the potential for harmful land uses to appear anywhere. Without zoning, a slaughterhouse, a nightclub with loud music, or a polluting factory could theoretically open next to a school or a quiet residential area. Proponents argue this would be handled by common law nuisance lawsuits, but critics say this is a reactive, costly, and inefficient solution compared to proactive rules.
  • Infrastructure Strain: A sudden, market-driven explosion of dense housing could overwhelm existing infrastructure—sewers, water lines, electricity, roads, and schools—if not carefully managed.
  • Loss of Community Character & Aesthetics: While a subjective point, many people value the look and feel of their neighborhood. Elimination could lead to unchecked development that erodes green spaces, blocks sunlight, and destroys historical architecture.
  • Potential for Increased Segregation: Ironically, a completely free market might lead to more economic segregation, as wealthy residents could use private covenants and homeowners' associations (HOAs) to create exclusionary enclaves, while low-income residents get pushed into areas with the worst negative externalities.

Conclusion

The case for eliminating zoning is fundamentally a case for radical deregulation based on a belief in free-market efficiency and absolute property rights. Proponents argue it would unleash a wave of construction that would solve housing affordability, make cities more dynamic and efficient, and roll back undue government overreach.

However, most practical urban policy experts advocate for a middle ground: significant zoning reform rather than elimination. This includes:

  • Abolishing single-family-only zoning.
  • Eliminating mandatory parking minimums.
  • Allowing "by-right" development that complies with clear, objective rules (e.g., height, bulk) to avoid political delays.
  • Using form-based codes that regulate the scale and form of buildings rather than their use, to avoid negative externalities while allowing mixed-use neighborhoods.

This approach seeks to capture the supply and affordability benefits of deregulation while maintaining a basic framework to manage nuisances and coordinate public infrastructure.

The Case for Abolishing Zoning: Restoring Freedom, Prosperity, and Justice

An Argument for Unrestricted Property Rights and Market-Driven Development

Introduction

Zoning laws are among the most destructive, economically ruinous, and morally indefensible policies in modern governance. Originally introduced in the early twentieth century—often with explicitly racist and classist motivations—zoning regulations have metastasized into a byzantine web of restrictions that strangle economic growth, perpetuate inequality, inflate housing costs, degrade the environment, and violate the fundamental property rights upon which free societies depend. The complete abolition of zoning laws would unleash an unprecedented era of innovation, affordability, community diversity, and individual liberty. Far from producing chaos, the removal of government land use restrictions would allow the natural organizing logic of markets, voluntary agreements, and organic community development to flourish—just as they did for most of human history and just as they continue to do in the few jurisdictions bold enough to reject the zoning paradigm.

This essay argues that all zoning laws should be abolished entirely, replaced by a system of unrestricted market-driven development and full property rights. The case rests on four pillars: moral principle, economic efficiency, social justice, and environmental sustainability.

I. The Moral Case: Property Rights as Foundational Liberty

The right to use one's property as one sees fit is not a peripheral concern in a free society—it is foundational. John Locke, whose philosophy profoundly shaped the American founding, argued that the protection of property is the primary purpose of government. When a government tells a landowner that she cannot build a duplex on her lot, cannot open a small shop in her neighborhood, or cannot construct housing above an arbitrary height limit, that government is engaged in a form of coercion that differs from outright confiscation only in degree, not in kind.

Zoning laws represent a massive, ongoing transfer of control from individuals to bureaucrats and politically connected interest groups. A homeowner who purchased property in good faith may find her plans for development blocked—not because those plans would harm anyone, but because a planning commission, influenced by the aesthetic preferences and economic anxieties of existing residents, has decided that the character of the neighborhood must be preserved in amber. This is not governance; it is the tyranny of incumbent interests over newcomers, of the politically powerful over the politically voiceless.

The moral argument is straightforward: if you own a piece of land, you should be free to build upon it, live upon it, and conduct commerce upon it, subject only to the constraint that you do not directly and demonstrably harm your neighbors through pollution, noise beyond reasonable levels, or genuine safety hazards. These constraints do not require zoning. They require tort law, nuisance law, and basic health and safety codes—legal mechanisms that long predate zoning and that function perfectly well without it.

The burden of proof must always fall on those who wish to restrict liberty, not on those who wish to exercise it. Zoning advocates have never met this burden. They offer speculative fears about what might happen in the absence of restrictions, while ignoring the very real, very measurable devastation that zoning has caused.

II. The Economic Case: Zoning as the Great Strangler of Prosperity

The economic costs of zoning are staggering and well-documented. Economists across the political spectrum—from the libertarian scholars at the Cato Institute to progressive economists like Nobel laureate Paul Krugman—have identified zoning as a primary driver of the housing affordability crisis, a significant drag on GDP growth, and a major impediment to labor mobility and economic dynamism.

A. The Housing Crisis

The most visible economic consequence of zoning is the housing crisis that afflicts virtually every major city in the developed world. In San Francisco, New York, London, Sydney, and countless other cities, housing costs have spiraled to levels that are crushing middle-class families, driving essential workers into hours-long commutes, and creating a new class of housing-insecure workers who earn decent wages but cannot afford a decent home.

The cause is not mysterious. When zoning laws mandate single-family homes on large lots, prohibit accessory dwelling units, cap building heights, impose minimum parking requirements, and require elaborate and time-consuming approval processes for any deviation from these restrictions, the supply of housing is artificially constrained. Elementary economics tells us what happens when demand rises and supply is held constant: prices soar.

Research by economists Chang-Tai Hsieh and Enrico Moretti, published in the American Economic Journal, estimated that zoning restrictions in just three cities—New York, San Francisco, and San Jose—lowered aggregate U.S. GDP by approximately 36 percent between 1964 and 2009. This is not a typo. By preventing workers from moving to the most productive cities—because they simply cannot afford housing there—zoning has cost the American economy trillions of dollars in lost output. This is an economic catastrophe of almost incomprehensible scale, and it is entirely self-inflicted.

Without zoning, developers would respond to price signals by building more housing where demand is highest. Apartments, townhouses, duplexes, micro-units, co-living spaces, and innovative housing forms not yet imagined would emerge to meet the needs of diverse populations. Prices would fall—not to zero, but to levels that reflect actual construction costs and land values rather than artificial scarcity created by political fiat.

B. The Destruction of Mixed-Use, Walkable Communities

Before zoning, most human settlements were naturally mixed-use. People lived above their shops, walked to work, and accessed daily necessities within their neighborhoods. Zoning destroyed this organic pattern by rigidly separating residential, commercial, and industrial uses. The result is the sprawling, car-dependent, socially isolating suburban landscape that defines modern American life.

This separation is not merely an aesthetic complaint—it is an enormous economic inefficiency. When homes must be miles from workplaces, shops, and services, the costs of transportation, infrastructure, and time multiply dramatically. Americans spend an average of nearly an hour per day commuting, a staggering waste of human potential that is directly attributable to zoning-induced sprawl.

In an unzoned market, the corner grocery store, the neighborhood café, the small professional office, and the residential apartment would coexist naturally, as they do in the most beloved and economically vibrant neighborhoods in the world—neighborhoods that, ironically, predate zoning and would be illegal to build under current zoning codes in most American cities.

C. The Entrepreneurial Tax

Zoning doesn't merely affect housing. It imposes enormous costs on small businesses and entrepreneurs. A person who wants to run a bakery out of her home, open a daycare center, or start a small manufacturing workshop faces a gauntlet of zoning approvals, variance hearings, and conditional use permits that can take months or years and cost tens of thousands of dollars in legal fees. Large corporations with dedicated legal departments can navigate this maze; individual entrepreneurs often cannot. Zoning thus serves as a regressive barrier to entry that protects established businesses from competition and prevents the creative destruction that drives economic progress.

D. Houston: The Existence Proof

Critics of abolishing zoning often claim that the result would be chaos. But we have a large-scale existence proof that this is not the case: Houston, Texas, the fourth-largest city in the United States, has never adopted a comprehensive zoning ordinance.

Houston is far from a dystopian wasteland. It is one of the most affordable major cities in America, with median housing costs dramatically lower than comparable cities with strict zoning. It is one of the most ethnically diverse cities in the country. It has vibrant neighborhoods, thriving businesses, world-class cultural institutions, and a booming economy that has attracted millions of new residents over the past several decades.

Does Houston have problems? Of course. Every city does. But its problems are not attributable to the absence of zoning—they are the ordinary challenges of rapid growth and urbanization. What Houston demonstrates conclusively is that a major modern city can function, thrive, and grow without zoning. The predicted disasters—chemical plants next to schools, factories in residential neighborhoods, total aesthetic collapse—have simply not materialized, because market forces, private covenants, and consumer preferences are far more powerful organizers of land use than zoning advocates acknowledge.

III. The Social Justice Case: Zoning as Institutionalized Exclusion

The history of zoning in America is inseparable from the history of racial and economic exclusion. The first comprehensive zoning ordinance in the United States, adopted by New York City in 1916, was motivated in significant part by the desire to prevent garment factories—staffed largely by immigrant workers—from encroaching on the fashionable retail districts of Fifth Avenue. Early zoning in many Southern cities was explicitly racial, designating certain blocks for white residents and others for Black residents. When the Supreme Court struck down explicitly racial zoning in Buchanan v. Warley (1917), cities quickly adopted facially neutral tools—single-family zoning, minimum lot sizes, minimum square footage requirements—that achieved the same exclusionary results by economic proxy.

This is not ancient history. The exclusionary effects of zoning are ongoing and devastating. Single-family zoning, which covers approximately 75 percent of residential land in most American cities, effectively prices out low-income and moderate-income families, who cannot afford single-family homes, from entire communities. It ensures that neighborhoods with the best schools, the safest streets, and the greatest economic opportunity remain enclaves of privilege, accessible only to those wealthy enough to pay the premium that artificial scarcity imposes.

The racial dimensions are stark. Exposed by scholars like Richard Rothstein in The Color of Law, the link between zoning and racial segregation is direct, documented, and damning. Zoning restrictions in affluent, predominantly white suburbs prevent the construction of apartments and affordable housing, perpetuating patterns of segregation that originated in explicitly racist policies and that continue to produce vast disparities in wealth, health, education, and opportunity.

Abolishing zoning would not instantly undo centuries of injustice, but it would remove one of the most powerful institutional mechanisms that perpetuates it. Without zoning, developers could build affordable housing in high-opportunity areas, diverse housing types could emerge in every neighborhood, and the artificial barriers that keep communities stratified by race and class would begin to dissolve.

The progressive defenders of zoning face an uncomfortable question: How can you claim to support racial justice, economic equality, and affordable housing while simultaneously defending the regulatory framework that is most responsible for perpetuating segregation and inflating housing costs? The contradiction is irreconcilable. True commitment to social justice demands the abolition of zoning.

IV. The Environmental Case: Zoning Causes Sprawl, and Sprawl Destroys the Environment

Environmentalists who support zoning are undermining their own cause. Zoning is the single greatest driver of suburban sprawl, and sprawl is an environmental catastrophe.

When zoning mandates low-density, single-family development and prohibits the compact, mixed-use neighborhoods that reduce automobile dependence, the result is a landscape that requires more driving, more road-building, more energy consumption, and more destruction of natural land. American metropolitan areas consume vastly more land per capita than their international counterparts, and zoning is a primary reason.

Consider the environmental implications: every acre of suburban sprawl was once forest, farmland, or wetland. Every mile of highway built to connect sprawling subdivisions to distant employment centers generates carbon emissions, fragments wildlife habitat, and increases impervious surface area that contributes to flooding and water pollution. Every mandatory parking space—and zoning codes often require multiple spaces per housing unit—is a patch of asphalt that absorbs heat, generates runoff, and occupies land that could be used for housing, parks, or natural systems.

Without zoning, market forces would naturally produce denser, more compact development in areas where demand is high. People who want to live in dense, walkable, transit-oriented neighborhoods—and surveys consistently show that a large and growing share of Americans do—would be able to do so, because developers would be free to build what the market demands. The result would be dramatically reduced per-capita carbon emissions, less destruction of natural land, and more efficient use of existing infrastructure.

The environmental argument for abolishing zoning is not speculative. Cities that allow greater density and mixed-use development have lower per-capita carbon footprints than sprawling, zoning-constrained cities. New York City residents, living in the densest urban environment in America, have per-capita carbon emissions roughly one-third the national average—not because New Yorkers are more virtuous, but because their built environment, shaped by density that predates modern zoning, makes low-carbon living the default.

V. Addressing Objections

The arguments against abolishing zoning generally fall into several categories, each of which collapses upon examination.

"Without zoning, someone will build a factory next to my house."

This objection reflects a fundamental misunderstanding of how markets and legal systems work. Even without zoning, property owners remain subject to nuisance law, which prohibits uses that create unreasonable interference with neighbors' enjoyment of their property. A factory belching toxic fumes next to a residential neighborhood would be actionable under nuisance law regardless of zoning status. Moreover, the market itself powerfully discourages incompatible uses. A factory built in a residential area would face higher land costs (residential land is typically more expensive than industrial land) and would gain no benefit from the location. The scenario is a bogeyman, not a realistic outcome.

In Houston, private deed restrictions and homeowner covenants provide an additional layer of protection, demonstrating that voluntary, market-based mechanisms can address legitimate concerns about incompatible uses without the heavy hand of government zoning.

"Property values will collapse."

This objection reveals the true motivation behind much zoning advocacy: the protection of incumbent homeowners' property values at the expense of everyone else. Zoning artificially inflates property values by restricting supply. When we say that abolishing zoning might reduce some property values, what we are really saying is that housing would become more affordable. For the millions of Americans who are currently priced out of homeownership or paying crushing rents, this is not a bug—it is the primary feature.

Moreover, the claim that all property values would decline is dubious. In many cases, allowing more intensive use of land—permitting a homeowner to build an accessory dwelling unit, for example, or allowing a commercial use on a ground floor—increases the value of the underlying property. The landowner gains options, and options have value.

"We need zoning to ensure orderly development."

History refutes this claim. The most beloved, orderly, and enduring neighborhoods in the world—the historic centers of European cities, the pre-zoning neighborhoods of American cities like Charleston, Savannah, Boston, and New Orleans—were built without zoning. They achieved their character through organic market processes, cultural norms, and the natural logic of human settlement. Zoning did not create order; it imposed a sterile, car-dependent, socially destructive version of order that most people, given a genuine choice, would reject.

"Some regulation is necessary."

This essay does not argue against all regulation. Building codes that ensure structural safety, fire codes that prevent catastrophic disasters, environmental regulations that prohibit pollution—these serve legitimate functions and do not require zoning. The argument is specifically against land use zoning: the government telling property owners what types of activities they may conduct and what types of structures they may build on their own land, absent any demonstrable harm to others.

VI. The Path Forward

Abolishing zoning entirely may seem radical, but it is increasingly recognized as necessary by scholars, economists, and policymakers across the political spectrum. The bipartisan consensus is growing. Progressive cities like Minneapolis have eliminated single-family zoning. Conservative states like Texas have long resisted comprehensive zoning. The YIMBY (Yes In My Back Yard) movement, spanning left and right, is building a powerful coalition around the recognition that zoning is a failed experiment.

The transition need not be instantaneous. A phased approach—first eliminating the most destructive restrictions (single-family-only zoning, minimum lot sizes, parking mandates, height limits), then progressively removing remaining use-based restrictions—could allow markets and communities to adjust. But the ultimate goal should be clear and uncompromising: the complete elimination of government zoning and the restoration of full property rights.

Private mechanisms—deed restrictions, homeowner association covenants, conservation easements, and voluntary neighborhood agreements—can address the legitimate concerns that zoning purports to serve, while preserving individual liberty and market dynamism. These mechanisms are superior to zoning because they are voluntary, negotiated, and flexible, rather than imposed, rigid, and politically captured.

Conclusion

Zoning is a century-old policy failure of extraordinary magnitude. It has inflated housing costs, deepened inequality, perpetuated racial segregation, destroyed the environment, strangled economic growth, and violated the fundamental right of individuals to use their own property. The evidence is overwhelming, the moral argument is clear, and the practical alternatives are proven.

The abolition of all zoning laws would not produce chaos. It would produce freedom—the freedom of individuals to build homes they can afford, the freedom of entrepreneurs to start businesses where opportunity exists, the freedom of communities to evolve organically rather than stagnate under the dead hand of bureaucratic control. It would produce a more prosperous, more equitable, more sustainable, and more dynamic society.

For too long, we have accepted zoning as an inevitable feature of modern governance, as natural and necessary as gravity. It is neither. It is a political choice—a bad one—and it can be reversed. The time to abolish zoning is now.

The strongest societies are those that trust their citizens with freedom. Zoning represents a profound failure of that trust. Let us restore it.

The Case for Zoning Freedom

A Speech Advocating for the Abolition of Zoning Laws

Ladies and gentlemen,

I want you to imagine something radical — and yet something that was the norm for most of American history. Imagine owning a piece of land and being free to build on it.

Not free to beg a planning commission. Not free to hire a lawyer to navigate thousands of pages of code. Not free to wait eighteen months for a permit that may never come. Actually, genuinely free.

That world existed. And we need to fight to bring it back.

The Broken Promise

We were told zoning would protect us — protect our neighborhoods, protect our home values, protect our quality of life. But let me ask you: protected for whom?

Because here's what zoning has actually delivered:

It has delivered a nation where a young teacher, a firefighter, a nurse — people we call essential — cannot afford to live in the communities they serve. It has delivered a housing shortage so severe that millions of Americans spend more than half their income just to keep a roof over their heads. It has delivered homelessness on a scale that should shame every city council member who ever voted to block an apartment building.

And it has delivered all of this not by accident, but by design.

Every single-family-only zone is a wall. Every minimum lot size is a gate. Every parking mandate, every setback requirement, every floor-area ratio — these are the bricks in a regulatory fortress built to keep housing scarce and prices high.

We didn't get here because the free market failed. We got here because we never let the free market work.

The Moral Case

Let me be direct about something that too often gets lost in policy debates: zoning is a profound violation of individual liberty.

You saved. You sacrificed. You purchased a piece of this earth. And then a group of bureaucrats and neighbors — people who have no ownership stake in your property — get to tell you what you can and cannot build on it.

They can tell you your home is too small. They can tell you your home is too tall. They can tell you that you cannot rent out your basement to a young couple struggling to get started in life. They can tell you that you cannot open a small shop on your own ground floor. They can tell you that the land your grandfather farmed cannot become homes for families who desperately need them.

This is not regulation. This is control. And in a free society, we should have the courage to call it what it is.

Property rights are not some abstract legal concept. They are the foundation of every other freedom we hold dear. When the government can dictate the use of your land without compensating you — when a zoning board can destroy the value of your property or prevent you from realizing its potential with the stroke of a pen — then property rights exist only on paper.

The great economist Ludwig von Mises once observed that the market economy means that the individual is free to choose the way in which he wants to integrate himself into the totality of society. Zoning takes that choice away — not just from builders and developers, but from every person who would have lived in the home that was never built, worked in the business that was never opened, walked to the corner store that was never permitted.

The Economic Case

Now, some will say: "This is idealism. The real world needs zoning."

Does it? Let's look at the real world.

Houston, Texas — the fourth-largest city in America — has no zoning code. And what happened? Did chaos reign? Did factories appear next to schools? Did neighborhoods collapse?

Houston isn't perfect. No city is. But it proves an essential point: the apocalyptic predictions of zoning advocates are wrong. Markets self-organize. Developers don't put industrial plants next to residential neighborhoods — because it would be economically irrational. Deed covenants, private agreements, and market forces accomplish what zoning claims to do, but without the coercion, without the bureaucracy, and without the devastating side effect of crushing housing supply.

Meanwhile, look at the most heavily zoned cities in America. Look at San Francisco, where a modest home costs over a million dollars. Look at Manhattan, where zoning has frozen neighborhoods in amber while people sleep on the streets below. Look at Los Angeles, where seventy-five percent of residential land is zoned exclusively for single-family homes in a metropolis of four million people.

These cities didn't zone their way to prosperity. They zoned their way to exclusion.

The research is overwhelming. Studies from economists across the political spectrum — from Edward Glaeser at Harvard to researchers at the Brookings Institution — estimate that zoning restrictions have reduced American economic output by trillions of dollars. Not billions. Trillions. By preventing people from moving to the most productive cities, by preventing housing from being built where demand is greatest, zoning has acted as a massive drag on growth, innovation, and opportunity.

Every unit of housing that is not built because of zoning is a family that doesn't form, a worker who doesn't relocate, an entrepreneur who doesn't start a business. The costs are invisible because they are borne by people who never got the chance — the young professional who never moved to the city with the best job, the immigrant family that never found an affordable apartment, the small business owner who never opened her doors.

The Social Justice Case

And here I want to speak plainly about something uncomfortable: the history of zoning in America is inseparable from the history of racial and economic exclusion.

The first comprehensive zoning ordinance in America — New York City, 1916 — was driven in part by the desire to keep garment factories, staffed largely by immigrants, away from the fashionable shops of Fifth Avenue.

Warley in 1917, exclusionary zoning became the tool of choice — achieving through economic means what could no longer be achieved through explicitly racial ones.

Minimum lot sizes. Single-family mandates. Bans on multifamily housing. These were not neutral planning tools. They were weapons — designed to ensure that certain people could not afford to live in certain places.

And they still work exactly as intended.

Today, in America, the most restrictively zoned communities are overwhelmingly wealthy and overwhelmingly white. The connection between zoning and segregation is not historical. It is ongoing.

Every time a suburban jurisdiction uses zoning to block apartments, it is pulling up the drawbridge. Every time a wealthy neighborhood downzones to "preserve character," it is saying — in the polite language of land use law — that newcomers are not welcome.

If we believe in equality of opportunity — truly believe in it — then we cannot defend a system whose primary function is to restrict opportunity based on geography and wealth.

Answering the Objections

Now, I know what the defenders of zoning will say. I have heard every objection, and I want to address them honestly.

"Without zoning, a factory could be built next to your house!"

You don't need a 3,000-page zoning code to stop a chemical plant from operating in a residential neighborhood. You need the common law principle that you cannot use your property in a way that directly harms others.

What zoning does beyond nuisance law is not prevent harm — it prevents choices. It prevents a homeowner from building an accessory dwelling unit. It prevents a neighborhood from having a corner café. It prevents a developer from building apartments where people want to live. These are not nuisances. "Property values will fall!"

It means: "I want the government to restrict what my neighbor can do with their property so that my property becomes more valuable through artificial scarcity." This is rent-seeking, pure and simple. It is using the coercive power of the state to transfer wealth from those who don't own property to those who do.

The places with the least zoning-like restrictions — the great pre-zoning neighborhoods of brownstone Brooklyn, Georgetown, the French Quarter — are among the most valuable real estate in America. They were built by the market. Zoning would have made them illegal.

"We need orderly development!"

Zoning killed that vitality. It separated uses into sterile pods — residential here, commercial there, industrial somewhere else — and in doing so, it created the car-dependent, soul-deadening sprawl that we now spend billions trying to undo.

It looks like more. More homes. More choices. More freedom. More opportunity.

It looks like neighborhoods where a young couple can find an apartment they can afford. Where a grandmother can build a small cottage in her backyard and age in place with dignity. Where an entrepreneur can open a bakery on the ground floor and live above it. Where a developer can build a beautiful apartment building on a transit corridor without spending five years in hearings.

It looks like cities that grow to meet demand — that welcome newcomers instead of walling them out. It looks like a housing market where supply can respond to need, where prices reflect reality rather than artificial scarcity.

It looks like communities shaped by the people who live in them — not by bureaucrats, not by NIMBYs at public hearings, not by a regulatory code that was written before most of us were born.

And yes, it will be imperfect. Markets are imperfect. Freedom is imperfect. But the imperfections of freedom are infinitely preferable to the planned cruelty of a system that tells millions of Americans: there is no room for you here.

The Call to Action

We stand at a moment of crisis. Housing costs are crushing the middle class. Homelessness is rising. Young people are giving up on the dream of homeownership. Essential workers are commuting two hours each way because they cannot afford to live where they work.

And at the root of all of it — all of it — is a regulatory system that makes it illegal to build the housing people need, where they need it.

Incrementalism has failed. "Zoning reform" has become an excuse for delay — a way for politicians to look busy while changing nothing. We don't need reform. We need abolition.

Abolish single-family zoning. Abolish use restrictions. Abolish density limits, height limits, minimum lot sizes, parking mandates, and floor-area ratios. Abolish the entire apparatus of land use control that has strangled our cities for a century.

Replace it with what works: strong nuisance law, building safety codes, environmental protections that address actual environmental harm, and the freedom of property owners to use their land as they see fit.

This is not a left-wing position or a right-wing position. It is a freedom position. It unites libertarians who believe in property rights with progressives who believe in housing justice. It unites economists who understand supply and demand with urbanists who love vibrant cities. It unites everyone who believes that in America, where you can live should not be determined by how much a zoning board likes your application.

The great housing crisis of our time was not caused by nature, or by fate, or by forces beyond our control. It was caused by law. By rules we wrote, by codes we adopted, by restrictions we imposed on ourselves.

And what law has broken, the repeal of law can fix.

Ladies and gentlemen, it is time to build. It is time to set our land — and our people — free.

Thank you.
